titre: “The Opium of the People”: What Marx Writes Before the Phrase
accroche: In 1843, Marx writes that religion is “the opium of the people.” The sentence before it says almost the opposite of an insult.
contenu_vulgarise:
“The opium of the people” is used today as a ready-made insult: it gets thrown at a believer like a diagnosis. Four words, one author, one verdict: religion lulls the poor to sleep so that the rich can sleep soundly. Yet the phrase comes from a text Marx wrote in 1843, and it lands in the middle of a paragraph that begins somewhere else.

## The Whole Paragraph

The text is the introduction to a critique of Hegel's philosophy of right, published in February 1844 in the *Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher*. Marx deals with religion there before moving on to politics. Here is the passage: “Religious misery is, on the one hand, the expression of real misery, and, on the other, the protest against real misery.” Religion is then called the sigh of the creature overwhelmed by misfortune, the soul of a heartless world, the spirit of a spiritless age, and only then does the phrase fall: the opium of the people.

The order matters. Marx does not begin by describing a poison the powerful pour into the glass of the poor. He describes real suffering, and a religion that is both its symptom and its lament. The image of opium, moreover, is not his own: the poet Novalis had used it in 1798, and Heinrich Heine in 1840. At the time, opium was also a medicine, prized for its soothing properties and feared for its power to cause dependence.

## What the Phrase Demands

The sentence that follows is far less often quoted: “The people's real happiness requires that religion be abolished as the people's illusory happiness.” Then: “To demand that they give up illusions about their situation is to demand that they give up a situation that needs illusions.” So Marx does not stop at consolation: he asks that we attack what makes it necessary.

This is not a defense of religion: he wants it abolished as illusory happiness. But his critique of it is, he writes, “in embryo, the critique of this vale of tears, of which religion is the halo.” That is the shift: read in its paragraph, the phrase does not stop at the believer. It points back to the state of the world that makes religion a necessity. To brandish it as a mere insult is to keep its last word and leave out the misery it took as its starting point.

carte.punch: “The opium of the people”: the sentence before it says almost the opposite of an insult.
carte.idee: In Marx (1843), religion is first “the expression of real misery” and “the protest” against it. The opium comes after. And the next sentence targets the situation that “needs illusions,” not just belief.

quiz.question: In Marx's text (1843), what immediately precedes the phrase “the opium of the people”?
choix: A call to ban churches in working-class neighborhoods
Religion described as protest and as the sigh of the overwhelmed creature
A defense of religious consolation as a remedy for misery
An accusation that the clergy preach resignation in exchange for a salary
quiz.explication: The text begins by making religion the expression of, and the protest against, real misery. It calls for no ban on churches, does not defend consolation as a remedy (it wants religion abolished as illusory happiness), and does not target the clergy in this paragraph.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In which publication does Marx's text appear, and when?
choix: In the Rhenish Gazette, in Cologne, in 1842
In the Communist Manifesto, in London, in 1848
In the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, in Paris, in February 1844
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text was published in February 1844 in the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher, in Paris, although it was written in 1843.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who, before Marx, had already used the image of opium in connection with religion?
choix: Hegel, in his lectures on the philosophy of right
Feuerbach, in The Essence of Christianity
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The poet Novalis had used this image in 1798, and Heinrich Heine in 1840, before Marx used it in 1843.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Marx demand right after writing that religion is the opium of the people?
choix: That the state fund secular alternatives to religious practice
That religion be abolished as the people's illusory happiness
That the Churches be separated from the state by law
That workers immediately stop all religious practice
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Marx writes that the people's real happiness requires that religion be abolished as illusory happiness, and not merely consoled.
